subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Why Coffee Smells So Good
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why Coffee Smells So Good usable.

hook.text: Coffee's aroma contains over 800 volatile compounds—more than almost any other food or drink.

buildup.text: The Maillard reaction during roasting creates furanones (caramel), pyrazines (nutty), and thiols (roasty).

discovery.text: Your nose detects aroma before your tongue tastes. Smell accounts for up to 80% of what you perceive as flavor.

twist.text: Brewed coffee smells better than it tastes because many aromatic compounds evaporate before reaching your mouth.

climax.text: That's why coffee-flavored foods often disappoint. They capture taste but miss the volatile aroma.

punchline.text: Coffee's best trick is its smell. 800 molecules, gone in seconds.

quiz.question: What percentage of coffee's perceived flavor comes from aroma?

details.summary: Roasted coffee contains over 800 volatile aromatic compounds, more than wine. The Maillard reaction during roasting creates complex molecules including furanones, pyrazines, and thiols that produce caramel, nutty, and fruity aromas. Aroma contributes more to perceived flavor than taste itself.
details.whyItMatters: Aroma is the primary way we experience coffee flavor. Most of what we call taste is actually smell detected by the olfactory system.
takeaways: Coffee contains over 800 identified aromatic compounds
Aroma contributes more to flavor perception than taste alone
Grinding releases the most intense burst of fresh aroma

faq.question: Why does freshly ground coffee smell so much better?
faq.answer: Grinding shatters cells and instantly releases trapped volatile compounds. Within minutes, many of these aromatics dissipate into the air. Whole beans protect these compounds inside their cell structure, which is why grinding just before brewing maximizes aroma.

faq.question: Why does coffee smell better than it tastes?
faq.answer: Many of coffee's most pleasant aromatic molecules are detected by smell but not by taste receptors. When we taste coffee, bitter and acidic compounds become prominent. The brain combines smell and taste into flavor, but the aromatic impression often exceeds the taste experience.
